pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of the shop in this workspace. Share it with the operations manager, the production supervisor, the quality inspector and whoever does purchasing.
: every quote and order with product, quantity, due date, total, runs, good units made and units still to make.
: the work orders. Each batch's work center, quality hold, units planned, good and scrapped, scrap rate, labor hours and checks.
: price, build hours, shop rate, material cost per unit, cost per unit and gross margin.
: the bill of materials. Each part and quantity in one unit of a product, with its cost.
: on hand, reorder point, lead time, supplier and unit cost.
: every inspection with its result, finding and disposition.
Monday: the production meeting; runs planned for the week.
Every day: runs updated, checks recorded, labor hours logged.
Wednesday: parts at reorder point ordered.
Friday: count the top five parts; review scrap and holds.
Every morning: runs on hold, runs starting today, orders due this week
Every week: reorder list, scrap by work center
Every month: unit costs updated, margins reviewed, full count
Every quarter: supplier review and price changes
The operations manager owns orders, pricing and purchasing. The production supervisor owns runs and labor. The quality inspector owns checks and holds. Everyone stops a run that looks wrong.

Guards stay on, push sticks are used, dust collection runs, and hearing and eye protection are worn on every machine. Any near miss is written up the same day, without blame, so the next person is safe.

Rename work centers, part kinds and product families to your shop, set your own shop rate per hour, and delete the sample rows once your own are in. Edit any cell in place; costs and margins update on their own.
The shop at a glance. Charts read the live tables.

Larkspur Cafe confirms 40 chairs due in three weeks. The supervisor plans two runs of 20, the first in four days. The recipe needs 560 board feet of walnut; 420 are on hand, so 200 more are ordered from the lumber yard with a nine-day lead time. The first run finishes with 19 good chairs and one scrapped for a crack; the second run is planned for 20, and the order ships on time.
Quality is cheapest at the start of a run. One careful first-article check saves a whole batch of rework. Every check is written down, and a failed check stops the run until it is understood.

: even coat, no runs, drips, dust or bare spots, color matches the sample.
: every unit, before packing. Wobble test on a flat surface for tables and chairs.

Find the cause, not the culprit: blade, jig, material moisture, finish temperature, or a step that is not written down.
When the fix is proven on a new unit, the inspector sets the hold to
: scrapped units over all units finished. Most small woodshops aim to keep it under about 3 percent. The Dashboard shows scrapped units by work center, which points at where to look first.
Material that moves after cutting, cracks or arrives wet is recorded and the supplier is told the same week, with photos. Two bad deliveries in a quarter is a conversation about changing supplier.
Every run on hold has a cause and a fix date
Scrap by work center against last month
Repeated findings turned into a written step or a jig

The bookshelf final inspection fails: one shelf has warped. The inspector puts the run on hold, scraps the shelf, and checks the lumber moisture: the last delivery reads 12 percent instead of 8. The supervisor stacks the remaining boards to acclimate for a week, the supplier is told, and the run is released when a remade shelf passes.
Running out of a five-dollar part can stop a five-thousand-dollar order. Reorder points, lead times and a weekly count keep the shop supplied without filling it with stock.
. A simple rule for the reorder point: what you use in a typical week, times the lead time in weeks, plus a week of safety. When on hand falls to the reorder point, order.
shows how far below it you are.
Every product's recipe lines say how much of each part one unit uses. Before confirming an order, multiply by the quantity and compare with what is on hand. The part's
count shows how many products depend on it; parts used everywhere (white oak, finish, glue) deserve a larger safety stock.

White oak is at 180 board feet against a reorder point of 300, with a nine-day lead time and two oak orders confirmed. The operations manager orders 600 board feet on Monday. The lumber yard's price rose a dollar a board foot, so the unit cost is updated, and the harvest table's margin drops three points; the next quote is priced up to match.
